![](images/92/924dcd7002fa679bf3a0021099928c45fba82a5bf54ba157a21d846eb1587640.svg)
lie on the $y$-axis. Since $e^{-4t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/c5/c5b1aa6ccde39c56b503e2d59a56e2ac8058b08495567f4e2cb40f6a056faedd.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t) = c_1e^{-t}$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{-4t}$ provided that $c_1,c_2 \neq 0.$ Then,

$$

$$

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_1=2$ with the eigenvector ![](images/b8/b8dce83f78184c194c43b2cf2b4148549a4ff0504a0f663f6a338a8cca6dec2f.svg) The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form

lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{unstable}}$ line.

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_2=4$ with the eigenvector ![](images/f9/f9da7bff2e0d90f112ce26291e3c1074e766e141bdae4198870d49136ed6706a.svg) The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
![](images/9d/9d8a16728992f0ce055be81c84ae0e905417e2ed74c4e659b277ab7f4226e90a.svg)
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{unstable}}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{an unstable node (source)}}.$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=7$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{7t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-6$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

${c}_{2}{e}^{-6t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-6t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?" :question/worked-solution "Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-7y(t)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4e6571d0-2b85-5e20-ad0d-0458eb1f4ac3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id - Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-5t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

![](images/df/df61bf017441f2dc3e34253d89f98f42cce2ec1b27131b9204952b059e335af8.png)

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-5t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-3t})^{′}}=\frac{-5{c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}}{-3{c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}}=\frac{5{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{5t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a saddle point}.$

:question/problem "$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Select the correct options below regarding the given decoupled system of linear differential equations.

$\,$
The $x$-axis is a {{field-1}} line.

$\,$
The $y$-axis is a {{field-2}} line.

$\,$
The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis and also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a stable node (sink)}.$ 

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:

node (source)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168020 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2<0$ (the opposite case, where $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2>0,$ is similar). 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/4d/4dc3aaf0f7dfd85070df84c13abe2cf02d85a704167569b3d3a76f2b58178c5b.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**.

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/76/76f6b9bbcdff2c87295fb0cd14dbdbbaa5e6c75eeb49c1cc158a4e8bd3da059d.svg) Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. This is called a **stable axis**.

Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **saddle point**.

In the phase portrait, we draw

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), while

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin).

A typical trajectory bends from the stable direction and then peels away along the unstable direction.

![](images/f2/f2538a59050e604d85fd9726e688cfbd2a5c9bdff4d15dd5ed465ed04f7290b4.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168002 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0.$ 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/75/75e7a0e16141db2a8da210c1ab30fc7328ccc98f861afec4db69d951ff3c9121.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin (*unstable axis*).

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/28/280e99a308962d43d1060be7100e294623d3bc3bfbe0579ab61d817695ad9e45.svg) Since $\lambda_2>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *away* from the origin (*unstable axis*).

Because both axes are *unstable*, the origin (equilibrium point) is called an **unstable node** or **source**.

In the phase portrait, we draw:

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), and

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin).

A typical trajectory for an *unstable node* emanates from the origin toward infinity. 

![](images/c9/c9f315c0b8a60a2c00e2f8e8e8b954214ce4d82cfd5832e15c26b429e29e535e.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168004 :tutorial/content "Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system
![](images/e1/e1efdd0b8c037c01450042384ce3bac663d0b549fa9557d0db09b692754cab0f.svg)

Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ 
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$

- *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.

- *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative).

Let's see some examples." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167013 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-6$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-6t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-2t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-6t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-6t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

"![](images/15/1515f63552e99b9ca9e1780f9689ac5d148969aaa1dccfc2ba55bcb87e534b34.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?" :question/worked-solution "Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-7y(t)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4e6571d0-2b85-5e20-ad0d-0458eb1f4ac3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-5t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/df/df61bf017441f2dc3e34253d89f98f42cce2ec1b27131b9204952b059e335af8.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-5t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-3t})^{′}}=\frac{-5{c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}}{-3{c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}}=\frac{5{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-5$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/36/362ee182f39f9d5cc1e7597f7e836a6ce802b4762a03c347c5701c0830f3d523.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-5t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-3t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-5t})^{′}}=\frac{-3{c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}}{-5{c}_{1}{e}^{-5t}}=\frac{3{c}_{2}}{5{c}_{1}}{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to \pm \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

{:db/id "question-637ffaff-c65f-5c9b-99c9-53a0db0e19a1" :question/id #uuid "637ffaff-c65f-5c9b-99c9-53a0db0e19a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-333211" :question/problem "$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Select the correct options below regarding the given decoupled system of linear differential equations.

$\,$
The $x$-axis is a {{field-1}} line.

$\,$
The $y$-axis is a {{field-2}} line.

$\,$
The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{5t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form

node (source)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168020 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2<0$ (the opposite case, where $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2>0,$ is similar). 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/4d/4dc3aaf0f7dfd85070df84c13abe2cf02d85a704167569b3d3a76f2b58178c5b.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**.

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/76/76f6b9bbcdff2c87295fb0cd14dbdbbaa5e6c75eeb49c1cc158a4e8bd3da059d.svg) Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. This is called a **stable axis**.

Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **saddle point**.

In the phase portrait, we draw

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), while

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin).

A typical trajectory bends from the stable direction and then peels away along the unstable direction.

![](images/f2/f2538a59050e604d85fd9726e688cfbd2a5c9bdff4d15dd5ed465ed04f7290b4.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168002 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0.$ 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/75/75e7a0e16141db2a8da210c1ab30fc7328ccc98f861afec4db69d951ff3c9121.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin (*unstable axis*).

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/28/280e99a308962d43d1060be7100e294623d3bc3bfbe0579ab61d817695ad9e45.svg) Since $\lambda_2>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *away* from the origin (*unstable axis*).

Because both axes are *unstable*, the origin (equilibrium point) is called an **unstable node** or **source**.

In the phase portrait, we draw:

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), and

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin).

A typical trajectory for an *unstable node* emanates from the origin toward infinity. 

![](images/c9/c9f315c0b8a60a2c00e2f8e8e8b954214ce4d82cfd5832e15c26b429e29e535e.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168004 :tutorial/content "Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system
![](images/e1/e1efdd0b8c037c01450042384ce3bac663d0b549fa9557d0db09b692754cab0f.svg)

Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ 
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$

- *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.

- *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative).

Let's see some examples." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167013 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186166536 :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?"] ["question-e04639b7-40d3-572d-8bb4-b806479b61ba" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-3t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-5t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](images/df/df61bf017441f2dc3e34253d89f98f42cce2ec1b27131b9204952b059e335af8.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-5t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-3t})^{′}}=\frac{-5{c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}}{-3{c}_{1}{e}^{-3t}}=\frac{5{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

![](images/11/11484704b873e4f4cb449e8eb452e0e4e2ceb71d9f2918b052d5f18cbdd7ca7b.png)"] ["question-e04639b7-40d3-572d-8bb4-b806479b61ba" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] :question/problem "$$

$$

The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}."] ["question-637ffaff-c65f-5c9b-99c9-53a0db0e19a1" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{5t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a saddle point}.$ 

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:

{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3y(t)\end{aligned}

The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}."] ["question-decb29d1-761c-5045-8201-b6cd8aa2cc30" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{an unstable node (source)}.$ 

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:

"question-2b822a97-2fd4-5c06-914f-271b7726501f"] [17592186168020 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2<0$ (the opposite case, where $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2>0,$ is similar). 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/4d/4dc3aaf0f7dfd85070df84c13abe2cf02d85a704167569b3d3a76f2b58178c5b.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**.

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{4t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Select the correct options below regarding the given decoupled system of linear differential equations.$\,$
The $x$-axis is a {{field-1}} line.

$\,$
The $y$-axis is a {{field-2}} line.

$\,$
The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-3$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a saddle point}.$

[{:db/id 17592186167843 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167997 :tutorial/content "Consider a *decoupled* linear system of ODEs
![](images/3f/3f7a114fa75100f8cd3ccf72822758e668f3a6a0824ad5f5437ebef138928fb5.svg)

In this lesson, we consider only decoupled systems with nonzero eigenvalues ![](images/77/77bce8fda831b5be2b2f52e043375447e794f8dad01a666d45e08716e912d707.svg) and ![](images/b8/b8ed089264b88bdcf4018f44db6dade448063b56a6ded558fb74d7c2ca61c0de.svg) so the origin is the equilibrium point we will classify.

Recall that the eigenvalues for a diagonal matrix are its diagonal entries, ![](images/77/77bce8fda831b5be2b2f52e043375447e794f8dad01a666d45e08716e912d707.svg) and ![](images/af/afb536c2c395100d85543d9c25f58d867e0bcfbd5f826d794284b648e7cc0550.svg) 
The corresponding eigenvectors are parallel to the coordinate axes:
![](images/83/8337ebfc4aae4b8e97438cdba58872082bdc8965932659fdf2f8ff9cf061b375.svg)

So, the general solution of the system is given by
![](images/fc/fcb5c1cea49dfe7aa1058f64d859a8b47c363f7f6195bf68056b18f1fa6d37f2.svg)

Notice that if a solution starts on one of the coordinate axes, it remains on that axis. These are called **straight-line solutions**:

- On the ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-axis (![](images/8d/8da7ef7a61d4c5af4d28575fcd263714cf3bda8e7d94985bd4bea5c03eb2d53f.svg)): 
![](images/aa/aa9cd3c49609ee6d09a61c9c31438e4297620feedfda1073fbc55c08e7c53d01.svg)

- On the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-axis (![](images/f2/f271ee76900762067d886b30871a9ea7538ae69318ad4514e5b39cfdce12644b.svg)):
![](images/50/509154a662b215d445b282396a8f43828e582d43282467a0da73843ade7ec5d8.svg)

The stability of these solutions as ![](images/91/919e9a7f2e074404c564846d6d8e1576e63b42ecbcc768b97d0632c645e32f22.svg) depends on the *signs* of the eigenvalues ![](images/77/77bce8fda831b5be2b2f52e043375447e794f8dad01a666d45e08716e912d707.svg) and ![](images/af/afb536c2c395100d85543d9c25f58d867e0bcfbd5f826d794284b648e7cc0550.svg) We will explore the three main stability cases in the upcoming examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "3ab2b715-abcc-511c-bbda-a2664d39efda" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14436 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a60bbebf-7d50-57b0-b823-f5cde68f6ecb" :step/math-academy-id 588112 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167852}} {:db/id 17592186167844 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168002 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0.$ 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin (*unstable axis*).

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ Since $\lambda_2>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *away* from the origin (*unstable axis*).

Because both axes are *unstable*, the origin (equilibrium point) is called an **unstable node** or **source**.

In the phase portrait, we draw:

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), and

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin).

A typical trajectory for an *unstable node* emanates from the origin toward infinity. 

![](images/c9/c9f315c0b8a60a2c00e2f8e8e8b954214ce4d82cfd5832e15c26b429e29e535e.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "302544e8-9eeb-5087-ae71-7143ffcbad9f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14460 :tutorial/title "Both Positive Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "752fcd7d-e772-51d0-84f5-e0724d157464" :step/math-academy-id 588113 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167845}} {:db/id 17592186167845 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168003 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system
![](images/3e/3e1a6630e46ba96ca21946d9feedc452d8416fe5bac17d5e8275c41c489d19ea.svg)
where ![](images/78/7853d8d4de1afb7f8899c60d7a5ea8e5ecd281594e48536c9f2d0bbef2c0301b.svg)

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-axis have the form ![](images/a1/a12ab1d3c69a589aa8de66fe8d14ed19b2938a9ef5591d87860e101a95afdc55.svg) Since ![](images/3d/3db8d2103adafd2be29df482295b07ef63576be6f152793463e034e808725edf.svg) we have that ![](images/bb/bb6223675110a379d33203ff637afaa6aefd3edf507b5a93386c608aa7aafca5.svg) as ![](images/e5/e54727d514ed264e6dd30c7f4044746e6d2b4b462dc3776daecf7eb68634c358.svg) Thus, the trajectories on the ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-axis move *toward* the origin (*stable axis*).

- The straight-line solutions on the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-axis have the form ![](images/aa/aae0f8015e0a575ca1e1fdbb37d011cbf78574649e3c9874163c3f14f1ca9929.svg) Since ![](images/23/23d0a8291d49cc1d2f0c6cff735a4d5214c2d9079dca67d803846af9b063358f.svg) we have that ![](images/69/69c464920e94e968ac5b2fe07f52d5e8a5e694f0fab6c9bfdcfd1b359a82e89e.svg) as ![](images/e5/e54727d514ed264e6dd30c7f4044746e6d2b4b462dc3776daecf7eb68634c358.svg) Thus, the trajectories on the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-axis move *toward* the origin (*stable axis*).

Because both axes are *stable*, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **stable node** or **sink**.

In the phase portrait, we draw

- arrows on the ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin), and

- arrows on the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin).

A typical trajectory flows into the origin.

Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ 
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$

- *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.

- *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative).

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "6fd81402-072b-5676-9cac-f53af20f3174" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14462 :tutorial/title "Classification of Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "b8abcadd-58fc-5f3e-a1a9-f6f32aaa7405" :step/math-academy-id 588125 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167851}} {:db/id 17592186167851 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166915 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166540 :question/id #uuid "4926ad20-fc6b-5a7d-80ee-aa39421c174d" :question/math-academy-id "e-21607"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "24bd917d-c4b3-5bf5-9426-a87a579b03c1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048990}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167200} {:db/id 17592186167236} {:db/id 17592186308409} {:db/id 17592186308410} {:db/id 17592186308411} {:db/id 17592186391158} {:db/id 17592186391169}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Decoupled Systems of Linear Differential Equations"} :step/id #uuid "6cadc020-1f0c-5e3d-88b7-c3977e63cc74" :step/math-academy-id 588126} {:db/id 17592186167852 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168020 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2<0$ (the opposite case, where $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2>0,$ is similar). 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**.

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. This is called a **stable axis**.

Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **saddle point**.

In the phase portrait, we draw

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), while

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin).

Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ 
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$

- *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.

- *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative).

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "6fd81402-072b-5676-9cac-f53af20f3174" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14462 :tutorial/title "Classification of Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "b8abcadd-58fc-5f3e-a1a9-f6f32aaa7405" :step/math-academy-id 588125 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167851}} {:db/id 17592186168004 :tutorial/content "Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.

- *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative).

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2<0$ (the opposite case, where $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2>0,$ is similar). 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**.

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. This is called a **stable axis**.

Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **saddle point**.

In the phase portrait, we draw

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), while

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin).

A typical trajectory bends from the stable direction and then peels away along the unstable direction.

"Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.
The course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ 
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$

- *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.

- *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative).
